newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia opposition presses on as court appeal fails.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition presses on as court appeal fails.

text.p: Serbian opposition parties lost a legal battle for control of Belgrade's urban government on Tuesday when the Yugoslav federal supreme court refused to hear their claims of election fraud by the ruling socialists.

As more than 100,000 supporters of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition demonstrated in the city, electoral commission chief Radomir Lazarevic said "all legal remedies were exhausted" as a result of the decision.

Opposition leaders termed the court's ruling unsurprising and they called on the international community to increase pressure on Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to force him into conceding election victory to the opposition.

"It would have been a miracle if this court had ruled otherwise," Zoran Djindjic, leader of the Democratic Party which is part of Zajedno, told Reuters. "This was just an illusion of justice from the start."

The United States and other Western governments have supported the opposition, cautioning against the use of force and backing their demands for socialist recognition of Zajedno's win with threats of reprisals.
"The only thing Milosevic cares about is international pressure, and it is for certain that in the next few days he will attempt to find a political solution," Djindjic added.

While the opposition vowed to maintain its daily demonstrations demanding the ouster of Milosevic, Yugoslav Federal Interior Minister Vukasin Jokanovic warned of a possible crackdown. "Demonstrations will be crushed if protesters use force," he told Reuters.

Zajedno leaders believe police infiltrators in the crowd could provide Milosevic with an excuse to break up the demonstrations which Jokanovic admitted contained "just enough police to do their job properly".
The opposition's majority in Belgrade and other main towns was disqualified in favour of the ruling socialists for unspecified "irregularities" in the November 17 election.
Zajedno deputies boycotted the federal parliament with the support of a small Montenegrin opposition party, vowing to stay away until Milosevic admitted he cheated them of victory.
The parliament session was the first since the socialists and their allies came within reach of a two-thirds majority in federal elections on November 3.

Although the opposition did not contest the legitimacy of the federal vote, Djindjic said: "Zajedno's 22 deputies will boycott all sessions of the federal parliament until the results of the (municipal) elections are recognised."
The federal election results gave Milosevic and his Montenegrin allies 84 of the 138 seats, eight short of a two thirds majority which would let him change the constitution.
Political sources said Milosevic would not find it hard to muster the votes he needed among the smaller parties to force through constitutional change to keep him in power.
His term as president expires next year and there has been speculation he could become federal president after turning it into an executive post modelled on France's powerful presidency.
The running conflict over the municipal election has upset this scenario, denting Milosevic's electoral credibility ahead of Serbian republic elections which must be held next year.
The United States and NATO issued separate condemnations of Milosevic on Tuesday and the alliance praised the opposition for ensuring that its demonstrations were peaceful.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, in Brussels for a meeting of NATO foreign ministers, warned that if Milosevic wanted to "rule Serbia as an unreformed dictatorship, it will only increase his isolation and the suffering of his people".
The remark was read as a clear hint that Washington would back the reimposition of U.N. sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia for 3-1/2 years during the war in Bosnia.
